 Inside the KOTRA-Chungdam Global Pop-Up Store
58 Brands on Display, Spanning K-Beauty and K-Food
Timed for Black Friday and Christmas, the Peak Shopping Season
Crowds From Day One, With 36,000 Visitors Expected
KOTRA: Sales Records Will Help Connect Firms With Local Buyers
 World | Published 2026.11.15. 23:52:21 | By Yoon Kyung-hwan ykh22@sedaily.com | Summary | Save A A A A man tries out Korean cosmetics at the American Dream Mall in New Jersey on Nov. 14, local time. New Jersey — Yoon Kyung-hwan, Correspondent NEW JERSEY — At American Dream, a sprawling mixed-use shopping mall in New Jersey, shoppers streamed in from the moment a Korean brand pop-up store opened on the 14th. The store was set up by Chungdam Global, a South Korean distribution company, with support from the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA). Visitors peppered staff with detailed questions about products and tried cosmetics on their faces and hands, repeatedly voicing their approval. Zea, an influencer who visited the store, said she loves Korean products. "American skin care often gives me breakouts, but that has never once happened with Korean products," she said.
 Chungdam Global and KOTRA opened the pop-up to introduce products from leading South Korean small and midsize companies to the U.S. East Coast ahead of Black Friday on the 27th and Christmas on Dec. 25, the biggest shopping period of the American year. It is also the first East Coast pop-up for K-brands opened by Kreassive, Chungdam Global's U.S. subsidiary. Sean Jang, Kreassive's co-chief executive, said the company had run pop-up stores only in California, on the West Coast, and was now looking for a way into the East.
 The event features 58 brands in total, including 49 in K-beauty and nine in K-food. Of those, 18 are South Korean small and midsize brands — 10 in beauty and eight in food. Sixteen brands, among them the skin care company DAMTIX and the sun care company SIABARRIER, are appearing in a U.S. brick-and-mortar store for the first time, drawing particular attention.
 KOTRA and Chungdam Global plan to run the pop-up from that day through Jan. 15 of next year. The store will sell about 18,000 items across roughly 200 product lines, along with some 1,300 kinds of official merchandise from more than 40 K-pop acts. Over the 63-day run, the two organizations are targeting 36,000 visitors, or about 570 a day, along with 8,900 paying customers, sales of 17,900 units and revenue of $260,000.
 Na Beom-geun, head of KOTRA's New York office, said the cost of running a standalone U.S. store is a heavy burden for an individual small or midsize company. "Based on the sales records built up at this pop-up, we will connect these firms to consultations with local buyers," Na said.
